solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Big name in oil, perhaps Aberdonian, too uppity to enter military unit

indicators.note: the reversed pair go into the oil company's initials, splitting B from P

parts.note: BP, formerly British Petroleum, is one of the giant oil companies

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from the bottom, i.e. backwards

parts.note: a Mac is a Scot, and an Aberdonian is one example
taken as written

explanation.surface: A Scottish oil executive is supposedly too arrogant to join the army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' flags the Aberdonian as just one example of a Scot; 'uppity' reverses both words, which suits a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: A training base where recruits are drilled hard is loosely a military establishment or unit.

clue.text: Name for Fascist the compiler clued as an anagram

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves, so this is I

indicators.note: the clue tells us outright that the word clued is to be rearranged

explanation.surface: The setter boasts of having disguised a dictator's title by scrambling it.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends to describe the clue itself; 'the compiler' is the setter speaking of themselves.
explanation.definitionFit: Mussolini, Italy's Fascist leader, was known by this Italian title, meaning 'the leader'.

clue.text: Marine's passing through party to mellow

indicators.note: the marine word travels through the middle of the phrase for party to, so it sits inside it

parts.note: to be party to something is to be in on it
marine relates to the sea, so 'marine's' gives the sea's, SEAS

explanation.surface: A marine at a party, or in on some plan, is urged to calm down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party to' looks like a gathering but is the phrase for being in on something.
explanation.definitionFit: Fruit that is ripe or at its prime is mellow, as produce is when properly seasonal.

clue.text: Make good, repairing halves of heart that's broken up

indicators.note: read as re-pairing: the two halves of the word for heart are paired again the other way round
the heart word is broken in two before its halves are swapped

parts.note: the heart of something is its core

explanation.surface: Someone vows to make amends by mending a broken heart.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'repairing' as re-pairing: the two halves of the heart word are put back together the other way round.
explanation.definitionFit: To make good a loss is to get back or compensate for it, a synonym.

clue.text: In analysis of stone circle, choose particle science

indicators.note: the word for choose sits inside the rearranged letters
an analysis breaks something down into its parts, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: to opt is to choose

explanation.surface: An archaeologist studying a stone circle must pick which particle science to use.
explanation.walkthrough: 'analysis of' rearranges STONE CIRCLE as ELECTRONICS, and 'In' puts OPT inside it after its eighth letter.
explanation.definitionFit: This branch of physics focuses beams of charged subatomic particles as light is focused, as in microscopes.

clue.text: See 5
Linesmen spraying part of Wandsworth

indicators.note: something sprayed is scattered about, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Line officials spray paint or water across a south London district.
explanation.walkthrough: Wandsworth is a London borough; this district, by Battersea, is home to the new US Embassy and the wholesale market.
explanation.definitionFit: This riverside area of south London lies within the borough of Wandsworth, so it is part of it.

clue.text: When papering over Mark's done with overall

indicators.note: the word for when covers over the other letters, which go inside it

parts.note: once can mean when, as in 'once you arrive'
NB, nota bene, means mark well; the 's is 'is'
a la, as in a dish done with a sauce, means in the style of or with

explanation.surface: A decorator, having wallpapered over a stain, declares the job finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mark' is the instruction 'mark well', nota bene; 'done with' is the cookery sense of a la, as in a dish done with a sauce.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking everything into account, as in 'overall it went well', is an idiomatic synonym.

clue.text: Polish Tintagel composer carries earls south-west

indicators.note: the composer's name holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: Arnold Bax wrote the tone poem Tintagel
E is an abbreviation for earl, so two earls give EE
SW is the compass abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Cornish-themed composer is pictured carrying noblemen off to the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: Tintagel is a Cornish castle site, hence south-west in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Wax made by bees is rubbed on furniture to shine it, so it is a polish.

clue.text: Artist's reduced application to face

indicators.note: the slang word for lipstick is cut short by its final letter

parts.note: lippie is informal for lipstick, applied to the face

explanation.surface: A painter's make-up has been toned down.
explanation.walkthrough: Lippie is British and Australian slang for lipstick.
explanation.definitionFit: Fra Filippo Lippi and his son Filippino were painters of the Italian Renaissance.

clue.text: Intriguing technique, for me, leads to narrative's denouement

definitions.text: Intriguing technique, for me, leads to narrative's denouement

indicators.note: intriguing, read as plotting, signals the letters are worked into a new order
a denouement is the ending, so the word's final letter is taken

explanation.surface: A writer of mysteries explains how her plotting drives the story to its resolution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intriguing' rearranges TECHNIQUE plus FOR ME; 'denouement' adds the last E of 'narrative'. Agatha Christie, so nicknamed, speaks the whole clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname of Agatha Christie, whose intriguing plots always end in a revealing denouement.

clue.text: Members bandy: 'Super? Finger? Salad?'

definitions.meaning: limbs that are curved outward at the knee
Super Bowl, finger bowl and salad bowl: these are bowl e.g.s, examples of a kind of dish

explanation.surface: Diners trade suggestions about which dish to serve.
explanation.walkthrough: Read the answer's letters as BOWL EGS: the three words are each an e.g. of a kind of bowl.
explanation.definitionFit: Legs curving outwards at the knee are bandy limbs, limbs being members of the body.

clue.text: In vehicle, promoted Cameron's birthday routine

indicators.note: the reversed title goes inside the vehicle

parts.note: a bus is a vehicle

indicators.note: in a down clue, promoted means raised up, so the letters read from bottom to top

parts.note: David Cameron was Prime Minister, PM; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A Prime Minister marks his birthday on a bus with some kind of routine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'promoted' works upwards in a down clue. Birthday bumps are a British custom of lifting the birthday person and bumping them on the ground once per year of age.
explanation.definitionFit: The custom of hoisting someone up and down once for each year is a familiar birthday ritual.

clue.text: One examining an employer

parts.note: per means a or an, as in 'ten pounds per head'
one who employs or uses something is a user

explanation.surface: A job applicant scrutinises a prospective boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employer' is read as one who employs, i.e. uses, a tool, not a boss.
explanation.definitionFit: To peruse is to read or inspect carefully, so one who does so is examining.

clue.text: King William's almost certain to stitch university fellow up

indicators.note: in a down clue the whole assembly is read upwards, i.e. backwards
the shortened word for certain is sewn around the other letters
almost means the word is not quite complete, losing its final letter

parts.note: certain means sure

explanation.surface: A medieval king is all but certain to betray a college don.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' trims SURE to SUR; 'to stitch' puts UF inside after S, SUFUR; 'up' reverses it. To stitch someone up is to frame them.
explanation.definitionFit: William II of England, son of the Conqueror, was nicknamed for his ruddy complexion.

clue.text: My tolerable first wife Maureen's accepted folio following impasse

indicators.note: the diminutive name takes in the phrase, which sits between its two letters

parts.note: Mo is a short form of Maureen; the 's is 'is'
said by the speaker, this is 'ex I can stand'
F is an abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: A man introduces Maureen as the one former wife he can bear, at a deadlock.
explanation.walkthrough: Turn 'My tolerable first wife' into the speaker's words, EX I CAN STAND; 'accepted' wraps MO round it.
explanation.definitionFit: A confrontation where no party can safely back down is a deadlock, hence a stalemate or impasse.

clue.text: See 20
Drive northwards to yield power to king

indicators.note: in a down clue, going north means reading upwards, so the letters run backwards

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king
to cede is to yield
P is the physics symbol for power
at can mean to, as in throw a stone at

explanation.surface: A road trip heading north gives way to a monarch's convoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'northwards' reverses K CEDE P AT. 'Drive' looks like a journey but is the machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A tape drive is the machine that runs magnetic tape for playback, a sound-system unit.

clue.text: With heat this biochemical process may imbalance homeostasis

indicators.note: to imbalance something is to upset it; the answer plus heat, upset, can make the long word

explanation.surface: A biology lesson warns that heat can disturb the body's steady state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'may imbalance' says the answer's letters plus HEAT rearrange to HOMEOSTASIS.
explanation.definitionFit: The passage of a solvent through a membrane from weaker to stronger solution is a biochemical process.

clue.text: With Mark 'O' losing it, seeing this?

indicators.note: the code word drops the letter it stands for

parts.note: Oscar is the radio alphabet word for O
someone losing their temper is said to be seeing red

explanation.surface: A man called Mark appears to fly into a rage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing it' does double duty: OSCAR loses O, and losing your temper is seeing RED.
explanation.definitionFit: Something bearing a blemish left by a healed wound has a mark, a synonym.

clue.text: A charge that is 'fabricated', I admitted (11)

indicators.note: the letter is let in among the rearranged ones
fabricated means made up, so these letters are made up into a new order

explanation.surface: A suspect confesses that an accusation was trumped up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fabricated' rearranges A CHARGE THAT IS, and 'admitted' lets I in. The definition is the answer to 11 Across.
explanation.definitionFit: The writer of Poirot and Miss Marple mysteries is widely called by that title.

clue.text: A new meal's presented without pastry

indicators.note: the meal word sits outside the other letters

parts.note: a dish is a meal; the 's is 'is'

explanation.surface: A fresh meal is served with no pastry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' means outside here, not lacking: D-AN-ISH.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet yeasted pastry, often with fruit or custard, is named after Denmark.

clue.text: 11 sped manically around stationary cars

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go round the traffic word
acting manically is acting wildly, so the letters are wildly rearranged

parts.note: a traffic jam is a line of stationary cars

explanation.surface: A crime writer drives frantically round a traffic queue.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the answer to 11 Across, the nickname shared by both themed crime writers.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of the Adam Dalgliesh novels was also hailed as a leading writer of crime fiction.

clue.text: Big cat fit — all bar tail — into grate

indicators.note: the shortened fit goes into the grating word

parts.note: to grate on the nerves is to jar

indicators.note: everything except the last letter is used

parts.note: an ague is a fit of shivering

explanation.surface: A big cat seems to suffer a fit by the fireplace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'all bar tail' trims AGUE to AGU, which 'into' places in JAR.
explanation.definitionFit: The large spotted cat of Central and South America is one of the big cats.

clue.text: Poetry about knights errant needs song parts restrained

indicators.note: the scrambled letters part the restrained word, sitting inside it

parts.note: chaste means restrained or modest

indicators.note: errant means wandering astray, so these letters stray into a new order

explanation.surface: Verse about wandering knights requires sections of song to be held back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'errant' looks like part of 'knights errant' but signals the anagram of NEEDS SONG; 'parts' means that rearranged run splits the restrained word.
explanation.definitionFit: These Old French epic poems recount the heroic deeds of knights such as Roland.

clue.text: See 1
See 7
Spiritual leader had upset across the main road

indicators.note: the main road stretches across the other letters, around them

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's main north-south motorway, written MI

indicators.note: upset means knocked about, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A religious leader was upset by having to cross a busy road.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' rearranges HAD to AHD, which the M1 (Britain's first motorway) spans.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islam, a messianic redeemer expected to come is given this title of a guided leader.

clue.text: In retrospect, failure to find a laptop is always this

indicators.note: looking back means the letters are read backwards

parts.note: to miss something is to fail to find it
a laptop is a PC, a personal computer

explanation.surface: Losing a laptop seems to be a constant problem.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin phrase, used in citations, means 'so throughout', i.e. thus everywhere, every time.
